extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, media scholars, journalism students, media critics
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate how PR- and wire-driven material shapes news production (churnalism), identifying the practical selection criteria newsrooms use and recommended reforms to restore independent reporting and verification. Useful for newsroom policy review, media-studies analysis, and journalism teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Churnalism (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The passive processing of material which overwhelmingly tends to be supplied for them by outsiders, particularly wire agencies and PR."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overarching diagnostic: when newsrooms primarily repackage externally supplied material rather than produce original reporting. Use this as a primary category to detect when newsroom output is dominated by pre-packaged content; look for patterns of minimal verification, heavy wire/PR sourcing, and desk-bound aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Cardiff study finding: large majority of published items are not original reporting (noted: 80% of stories in Britain's quality press were not original; only 12% of stories generated by reporters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metric for evaluating newsroom health: proportion of pieces that originate from reporters' own reporting versus recycled wire/PR. Targets or benchmarks can be set (e.g., increase reporter-generated percentage). Use story-origin audits to measure progress and identify beats that have become mere aggregators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing reliance (wire services, press releases, PR agencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heavy reliance on wire services (Reuters, AP, AFP, PA), press releases, PR agency material, and other media's reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and log primary sources for published pieces. High percentages of external sourcing indicate churnalism. Guidance: diversify sourcing, prioritize independent sources, and track whether a story depends on a single PR/wire feed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Already-packaged content as newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: News selection driven by 'already-packaged' content such as press releases and wire copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: treating packaging as a proxy for news value. Editors should distinguish package convenience from public-interest importance; require added reporting/context when using packaged content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick turnaround capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are selected because they can be turned around quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speed-over-depth incentive: prioritize stories that can be published with minimal reporting time. Recommendation: balance fast coverage with standards for verification and context; flag 'fast but unverified' items for later follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification not required (officiality bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Material that requires no verification because it is presented as 'official' (e.g., press releases, wire copy) is more likely to be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: treating official-sounding content as verified. Editorial policy should require explicit verification steps or transparent labelling when content is published without independent corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source supplies it free (cost bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are favored when the source supplies the material at no cost to the newsroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic incentive skews selection toward free, PR-supplied material. Track and disclose when content originated as free supply; consider the hidden cost of eroded editorial independence and invest resources in original reporting where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filling space over informing (space-filling selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication driven more by the need to fill pages/slots than by informing the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial evaluation should ask whether a piece serves public interest or simply fills space. Adopt newsroom quotas or editorial checks that prioritize substance over volume and reduce trivial 'space-filling' outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Following the pack (herd behaviour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms follow other outlets' reporting ('the pack'), republishing or echoing material rather than investigating independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect herd patterns by tracing lead stories' origins across outlets. Encourage beats to pursue original angles and cross-check sources rather than defaulting to what competitors publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding original investigation (cost/effort avoidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial practice of avoiding original investigation because it is costly and time-consuming; beat reporting becomes desk-bound aggregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: expecting reporters to produce high volumes of copy without resources for investigation. Reform by restoring investigative time allocation, lowering per-reporter output demands, and incentivizing original reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staffing and resource levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes of churnalism include staff cuts, spending cuts, and increased output demands per reporter, resulting in loss of investigative capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use staffing/resource audits as part of newsroom evaluation. Policies should consider staff-to-output ratios, budget allocations for investigative work, and the impact of consolidation on editorial quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial judgment narrowed to print/no-print decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial decision-making becomes limited to whether to print a supplied item rather than what to investigate or prioritize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess editorial workflows: if choices are primarily binary about running supplied copy, broaden decision criteria to include public interest, originality, and required verification; restore active editorial commissioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform recommendation: be transparent about where material comes from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial policies should require clear sourcing statements in copy (e.g., 'based on a press release from X' or 'according to wire service Y') and maintain logs of source origins for internal review and public accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure when content is press-release-derived
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform recommendation: explicitly disclose when published content derives from press releases or PR material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt labelling practices and staff guidance to flag press-release-derived pieces for readers; consider correcting or augmenting such pieces with independent reporting where warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification standards / fact-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform recommendation: restore or adopt verification standards so that PR/wire material is independently checked before publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish minimum verification protocols for different content types (e.g., immediate labelling for unverified wire copy; mandatory corroboration for claims of wrongdoing). Train staff and allocate time/resources for verification tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to original reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform recommendation: recommit newsroom resources and editorial priorities to original reporting rather than passive reprinting of supplied material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set explicit editorial goals for reporter-originated stories, protect reporters' time for fieldwork, and create incentives/reward structures for investigative work and scoops.

rubrics_metrics.name: News selection becomes PR-agenda rationalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Implication: news values are often rationalizations of the PR-supplied agenda — 'newsworthy' can mean 'supplied by a reliable PR shop.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use critical audits to reveal instances where PR agendas shape coverage. Introduce editorial checks that interrogate whether a topic's newsworthiness stems from public interest rather than PR prominence.
